message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, no mold, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If the landlord fails to fix a serious issue, you may withhold rent or repair‑and‑deduct (but only after giving notice). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice if you’re not sure. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the term ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the court process: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days) for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend any court hearing; you can present evidence of your rights. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to repair a problem and deduct the cost from rent **only** if the landlord fails to fix it after notice. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Generally allowed if the lease permits it or if the landlord consents. | • Get written permission. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified. | • Verify which utilities you’re responsible for. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Consider a basic policy covering personal property and liability. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division.
• Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs.
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). | • Use these resources for disputes or to file complaints. | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document the condition** – take dated photos or video of every room, appliances, and any existing damage. 3. **Get a written receipt** for the security deposit and any initial rent payment. 4. **Ask for a copy of the landlord’s contact information** and any required disclosures (e.g., lead paint). ### When Problems Arise 1. **Notify the landlord in writing** (email or certified mail). 2. **Keep copies** of all correspondence. 3. **Give the landlord a reasonable time** to fix the issue (usually 10–14 days). 4. **If unresolved**, consider: - Withholding rent (after giving notice). - Repair‑and‑deduct (document everything). - Filing a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. - Seeking legal counsel or mediation. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for rent payment and lease termination. If you encounter issues, document everything, communicate in writing, and use the available state resources to protect your rights.
